No matter what any man's endowments might be; no matter what might be his wealth, his standing, or his talent; no matter if he were regarded as a ruler in the church, or at the head of a party; yet, if he had not true love to the Lord Jesus, he could not be saved. This sentiment is in accordance with the declaration of the Scripture everywhere. See, particularly, Jn 3:36, Mk 16:16; Mk 16:16.

Maran-atha. These are Syriac words, Moran Etho--" the Lord comes;" .i.e., will come. The reason why this expression is added may be,

(1.) to give the greater solemnity to the declaration of the apostle; i. e.,. to give it an emphatic form.

(2.) To intimate that, though there were no earthly power to punish a want of love to the Saviour; though the state could not, and ought not to punish it; and though the church could not exclude all who did not love the Lord Jesus from its bosom, yet they could not escape. For the Lord would himself come to take vengeance on his enemies; and no one could escape. Though, therefore, those who did not love the Lord Jesus could not be punished by men, yet they could not escape Divine condemnation. The Lord would come to execute vengeance himself, and they could not escape. It is probable (see Lightfoot in loco) that the Jews were accustomed to use such a form in their greater excommunication; and that they meant by it, that the person who was thus devoted to destruction, and excommunicated, must be destroyed; for the Lord would come to take vengeance on all his enemies. "It certainly was not now, for the first time, used as a new kind of cursing by the apostle; but was the application of a current mode of speech to the purpose he had in contemplation. Perhaps, therefore, by inspecting the manners of the East, we may illustrate the import of this singular passage. The nearest approach to it that I have been able to discover, is in the following extract from Mr. Bruce; and though, perhaps, this does not come up to the full power of the apostle's meaning, yet, probably, it gives the idea which was commonly attached to the phrase among the public. Mr. Bruce had been forced by a pretended saint, in Egypt, to take him on board his vessel, as if to carry him to a certain place--whereas, Mr. Bruce meant no such thing; but, having set him on shore at some little distance from whence he came, 'we slacked our vessel down the stream a few yards, filling our sails, and stretching away. On seeing this, our saint fell into a desperate passion, cursing, blaspheming, and stamping with his feet; at every word crying, "Shar Ulah!" i.e., May God send, and do justice!' This appears to be the strongest execration this passionate Arab could use; i.e., 'To punish you adequately is out of my power: I remit you to the vengeance of God.' Is not this the import of anathema maranatha?" -- Taylor, in Calmet. This solemn declaration, or denunciation, the apostle wrote with his own hand, as the summary of all that he had said, in order that it might be attentively regarded. There is not a more solemn declaration in the Bible; there is not a more fearful denunciation; there is no one that will be more certainly executed. No matter what we may have--be it wealth, or beauty, or rigour, or accomplishment, or adorning, or the praise and flattery of the world; no matter if we are elevated high in office and in rank; no matter if we are honoured by the present age, or gain a reputation to be transmitted to future times; yet, if we have not love to the Saviour, we cannot be saved. We must be devoted to the curse; and the Lord Jesus will soon return to execute the tremendous sentence on a guilty world. How important, then, to ask whether we have that love? Whether we are attached to the Lord Jesus in such a manner as to secure his approbation? Whether we so love him as to be prepared to hail his coming with joy, and to be received into his everlasting kingdom. In the close of the Notes on this epistle, I may ask any one who shall read these pages, whether he has this love? And I may press it upon the attention of each one, though I may never see his face in the flesh, as the great inquiry which is to determine his everlasting destiny. The solemn declaration stands here, that if he does not love the Lord Jesus, he will be, and he ought to be, devoted to destruction. The Lord Jesus will soon return to make investigation, and to judge the world, There will be no escape; and no tongue can express the awful horrors of an ETERNAL CURSE, PRONOUNCED BY THE LIPS OF THE SON OF GOD!

(a) "love not the Lord Jesus" Eph 6:24 (b) "Anathema Maran-atha" Gal 1:8,9 (c) "Maran-atha" Jude 1:14,15
entries.e3ea4071eac27d2ac59596848d01e1dcc40baf77:
Verse 23. The grace, etc. Rom 16:20.

(d) "grace of" Rom 16:20
entries.9abd89d939bb42b39088a9e04c2d89cee9d1121a:
Verse 24. In Christ Jesus. Through Christ Jesus; or in connexion with your love to him; i.e., as Christians. This is an expression of tender regard to them as Christian brethren; of his love for the church; and his earnest desire for their welfare. It is in accordance with the usual manner in which he closes his epistles; and it is peculiarly tender, affectionate, and beautiful here, when we consider the manner in which he had been treated by many of the Corinthians; and as following the solemn declaration in 1Cor 16:22. Paul loved them; loved them intensely, and was ever ready to express his affectionate regard for them all, and his earnest desire for their salvation.

The subscription to the epistle, "The first epistle to the Corinthians," etc., was evidently written by some other hand than that of Paul, and has no claim to be regarded as inspired. Probably these subscriptions were added a considerable time after the epistles were first written; and in some instances evidently by some person who was not well informed on the subject. See the Note at the end of the Epistle to the Romans. In this instance, the subscription is evidently in its main statement false. The epistle bears internal marks that it was written from Ephesus, though there is every probability that it was sent by three of the persons who are here mentioned. It is absurd, however, to suppose that Timothy was concerned in bearing the epistle to them, since it is evident, that when it was written he was already on a visit to the churches, and on his way to Corinth. 1Cor 16:10, 1Cor 16:11; 1Cor 4:17. There is not the slightest internal evidence that it was written from Philippi; but everything in the epistle concurs in the supposition that it was sent from Ephesus. See the Introduction to the epistle. There is, however, a considerable variety among the Mss. in regard to the subscription. They are evidently none of them of any authority; and as these subscriptions generally mislead the reader of the Bible, it would have been better had they been omitted.

entries.1390679923c3ac0bcbd782505c9ebaef1ff35c5c: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.16.1" sID="gen120486" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120487" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">But concerning the collection</hi> Luke relates (<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.11.28">Acts 11:28</reference>) that the prediction of Agabus, foretelling that there would be a famine under Claudius Caesar, gave occasion for alms being collected by the saints, with the view of affording help to the brethren in Jerusalem. For though the Prophet had foretold, that this calamity would be generally prevalent almost throughout the world, yet as they were more heavily oppressed with penury at Jerusalem, and as all the Gentile Churches were bound, if they would not be held guilty of very great ingratitude, to afford aid to that place from which they had received the gospel, every one, consequently, forgetful of self, resolved to afford relief to Jerusalem. That the pressure of want was felt heavily at Jerusalem, appears from the Epistle to the Galatians, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gal.2.10">Galatians 2:10</reference>,) where Paul relates, that he had been charged by the Apostles to stir up the Gentiles to afford help. <note n="149"> <div sID="gen120488" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">D’inciter les Gentiles a subuenir a la pourete qui y estoit</foreign>;” — “To stir up the Gentiles to relieve the poverty that existed there.”<div eID="gen120488" type="x-p"/> </note> Now the Apostles would never have given such a charge, had they not been constrained by necessity. Farther, this passage is an evidence of the truth of what Paul states there also — that he had been careful to exhort the Gentiles to afford help in such a case of necessity. Now, however, he prescribes the method of relief; and that the Corinthians may accede to it the more readily, he mentions that he had already prescribed it to the Churches of Galatia; for they would necessarily be the more influenced by example, as we are wont to feel a natural backwardness to anything that is not ordinarily practiced. Now follows the method — by which he designed to cut off all hinderances and impediments.<div eID="gen120487" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120486" osisID="1Cor.16.1" type="section"/>
entries.30b36decbc0e90dc686ac9b6e1a99368d497dd42: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.16.2" sID="gen120489" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120490" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi> <hi type="italic">On one of the Sabbaths.</hi> The end is this — that they may have their alms ready in time. He therefore exhorts them not to wait till he came, as anything that is done suddenly, and in a bustle, is not done well, but to contribute on the Sabbath what might seem good, and according as every one’s ability might enable — that is, on the day on which they held their sacred assemblies. The clause rendered on <hi type="italic">one of the Sabbaths, (</hi><foreign xml:lang="el">κατὰ μίαν σαββάτων</foreign><hi type="italic">,) </hi>Chrysostom explains to mean — <hi type="italic">the first Sabbath. </hi>In this I do not agree with him; for Paul means rather that they should contribute, one on one Sabbath and another on another; or even each of them every Sabbath, if they chose. For he has an eye, first of all, to convenience, and farther, that the sacred assembly, in which the communion of saints is celebrated, might be an additional spur to them. Nor am I more inclined to admit the view taken by Chrysostom — that the term <hi type="italic">Sabbath </hi>is employed here to mean the <hi type="italic">Lord’s day, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Rev.1.10">Revelation 1:10</reference>,) for the probability is, that the Apostles, at the beginning, retained the day that was already in use, but that afterwards, constrained by the superstition of the <hi type="italic">Jews, </hi>they set aside that day, and substituted another. Now the <hi type="italic">Lord’s day </hi>was made choice of, chiefly because our Lord’s <hi type="italic">resurrection </hi>put an end to the shadows of the law. Hence the day itself puts us in mind of our Christian liberty. We may, however, very readily infer from this passage, that believers have always had a certain day of rest from labor — not as if the worship of God consisted in idleness, but because it is of importance for the common harmony, that a certain day should be appointed for holding sacred assemblies, as they cannot be held every day. For as to Paul’s forbidding elsewhere (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gal.4.10">Galatians 4:10</reference>) that any distinction should be made between one day and another, <hi type="italic">that </hi>must be understood to be with a view to religion, <note n="150"> <div sID="gen120491" type="x-p"/> See Calvin’s Institutes, volume 1.<div eID="gen120491" type="x-p"/> </note> and not with a view to polity or external order. <note n="151"> <div sID="gen120492" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Quand on le fait pour deuotion, comme cela estant vn seruice de Dieu, et non pas pour la police externe</foreign>;” — “When it is done for the sake of devotion, as though it were a service done to God, and not with a view to external polity’.”<div eID="gen120492" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120493" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Treasuring up</hi> I have preferred to retain the Greek <hi type="italic">participle, </hi>as it appeared to me to be more emphatic. <note n="152"> <div sID="gen120494" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">On a par ci deuant traduit, <hi type="italic">amassant; </hi>mais i’ay mieux aired retenir la propriete du mot Grec</foreign>;” — “The word before us has been rendered <hi type="italic">laying up; </hi>but I have preferred to retain the peculiar force of the Greek word.”<div eID="gen120494" type="x-p"/> </note> For although <foreign xml:lang="el">θησανρίζειν</foreign> means to <hi type="italic">lay up, </hi>yet in my opinion, he designed to admonish the Corinthians, that whatever they might contribute for the saints would be their best and safest <hi type="italic">treasure. </hi>For if a heathen poet could say — “What riches you give away, those alone you shall always <hi type="italic">have,</hi> <note n="153"> <div sID="gen120495" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="la">Quas dederis, solas semper habebis opes</foreign>.” (Martial. Epage 5:42.) A similar sentiment occurs in the writings of the poet <hi type="italic">Rabirius. “</hi><foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">Hoc </hi>habeo, luodeunque dedi</foreign>;<hi type="italic">”</hi> — <hi type="italic">“</hi>I have whatever I have given away.” (See <hi type="italic">Seneca, </hi>ib. 6, de Beneft) Alexander the Great, (as stated by <hi type="italic">­Plutarch,) </hi>when asked where he had laid up his <hi type="italic">treasures, </hi>answered, <hi type="italic">“</hi><foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">Apud </hi>amicos</foreign>;<hi type="italic">”</hi> — “Among my friends.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120495" type="x-p"/> </note> how much more ought that consideration to have influence among us, who are not dependent on the gratitude of men, but have God to look to, who makes himself a debtor in the room of the poor man, to restore to us one day, with large interest, whatever we give away? (<reference osisRef="Bible:Prov.19.17">Proverbs 19:17</reference>.) Hence this statement of Paul corresponds with that saying of Christ —<div eID="gen120493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120496" type="x-p"/>Lay up for yourselves treasure in heaven, where it will not be exposed either to thieves, or to moths. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.20">Matthew 6:20</reference>.)<div eID="gen120496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120497" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">According as he has prospered.</hi> Instead of this the old translation has rendered it, <hi type="italic">What may seem good to him, </hi>misled, no doubt, by the resemblance between the word made use of, and another. <note n="154"> <div sID="gen120498" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">“</hi><foreign xml:lang="fr"><hi type="italic">S’abusant </hi>a l’affinite des deux mots Grecs</foreign>;<hi type="italic">”</hi> — <hi type="italic">“</hi>Misled by the resemblance between two Greek words.” Calvin’s meaning seems to be that the verb <foreign xml:lang="el">εὐοδόομαι</foreign>, <hi type="italic">(to be prospered,) </hi>made use of here by Paul, had been confounded with <foreign xml:lang="el">εὐδοκέω</foreign> <hi type="italic">(to seem good.) </hi>Wiclif (1380) in accordance with the Vulgate, renders as <hi type="italic">follows</hi> — <hi type="italic">Kepynge that that plesith to </hi>hym. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120498" type="x-p"/> </note> Erasmus renders it, <hi type="italic">What will be convenient.</hi> <note n="155"> <div sID="gen120499" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">C’est a dire, selon sa commodite</foreign>;” — “That is to say, according to his convenience.”<div eID="gen120499" type="x-p"/> </note> Neither the one nor the other pleased me, for this reason — that the proper signification of the word brings out a meaning that is much more suitable; for it means — to <hi type="italic">go on prosperously. </hi>Hence he calls every one to consider his ability — “Let every one, according as God hath blessed him, lay out upon the poor from his increase.”<div eID="gen120497" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120489" osisID="1Cor.16.2" type="section"/>
entries.4ab320377d9577b8a5140c4c89fbf652fddfd079: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.16.3" sID="gen120500" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120501" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi> <hi type="italic">And when I come</hi> As we are cheerful in giving, when we know for certain, that what we give is well laid out, he points out to the Corinthians a method, by which they may be assured of a good and faithful administration — by selecting approved persons, to whom they may intrust the matter. Nay more, he offers his own services, if desired, which is an evidence that he has the matter at heart.<div eID="gen120501" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.3" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120500" osisID="1Cor.16.3" type="section"/>
entries.b868ebc29869643bfdcdab733f71b4481d947ff6:
5. When I shall pass through Macedonia The common opinion is, that this espistle was sent from Philippi. Persons coming thence to Corinth by land, required to pass through Macedonia; for that colony is situated in the farthest extremity, towards the Emathian mountains. Paul, it is true, might, instead of going by land, have gone thither by sea, but he was desirous to visit the Macedonian Churches, that he might confirm them in passing. So much for the common opinion. To me, however, it appears more probable, that the epistle was written at Ephesus; for he says a little afterwards, that he will remain there until Pentecost, (1 Corinthians 16:8)
“St. Paul was now at Ephesus; for almost all allow, in opposition to the subscription at the end of this epistle, that states it to have been written from Philippi, that it was written from Ephesus; and this is supported by many strong arguments; and the 8th verse here seems to put it past all question: I will tarry at Ephesus; i.e., I am in Ephesus, and here I purpose to remain until Pentecost.” — Dr. Adam Clarke.nEd.
; and he salutes the Corinthians, not in the name of the Philippians, but of the Asiatics. (1 Corinthians 16:19.)
“The Churches of Asia salute you, i.e., the Churches in Asia Minor. Ephesus was in this Asia, and it is clear from this that the Apostle was not at Philippi. Had he been at Philippi, as the subscription states, he would have said, The Churches of Macedonia, not the Churches of Asia, salute you.” — Dr. Adam Clarke. — Ed.
Besides, in the second epistle he explicitly states, that, after he had sent away this epistle, he passed over into Macedonia. (2 Corinthians 2:13.) Now after passing through Macedonia, he would be at a distance from Ephesus, and in the neighborhood of Achaia. Hence I have no doubt that he was at Ephesus at that time: thence he could sail by a straight course to Achaia. For visiting Macedonia, a long circuit was needed, and a more disagreeable route. Accordingly he lets them know that he will not come to them by a direct course, as he required to go through Macedonia
To the Corinthians, however, he promises something farther — that he would make a longer stay with them By this he shows his affection towards them. For what reason had he for delay, except that he was concerned as to their welfare? On the other hand, he lets them know how fully assured he is of their affection towards him in return, by taking it, as it were, for granted that he would be conducted forward by them in the way of kindness; for he says this from confidence in their friendship.
“Ils le conduiront par tout ou il ira;” — “They will conduct him forward wherever he may go.”
After saying everything, however, he subjoins this limitation — if the Lord permit With this reservation, saints ought to follow up all their plans and deliberations; for it is an instance of great rashness to undertake and determine many things for the future, while we have not even a moment in our power. The main thing indeed is, that, in the inward affection of the mind, we submit to God and his providence, whatever we resolve upon;
“Tout ce que nous entreprenons et consultons;” — “Everything that we undertake and resolve upon.”
but at the same time, it is becoming that we should accustom ourselves to such forms of expression, that whenever we have to do with what is future we may make everything depend on the divine will.
“De remettre a la volonte de Dieu tout ce que nous entreprendrons pour le temps aduenir;” — “So as to give up to the will of God everything that we shall undertake for the time to come.
1 Corinthians 16:8-12
8. But I will tarry at Ephesus until Pentecost.
8. Commorabor autem Ephesi usque ad Pentecosten.
9. For a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries.
9. Nam ostium milli aperture est magnum et efficax, et
“Et, ou mais, il y a;” — “And, or but, there are.”
adversarii multi.
10. Now if Timotheus come, see that he may be with you without fear: for he worketh the work of the Lord, as I also do
10. Quodsi venerit Timotheus, videte, ut absque metu sit apud vos: opus enim Domini operatur, quemadmodum et ego.
11. Let no man therefore despise him: but conduct him forth in peace, that he may come unto me: for I look for him with the brethren.
11. Ne quis igitur eum spernat: sed prosequamini eum cum pace,
“En paix (ou, seurete);” — “In peace (or, safety.)”
ut veniat ad me: exspecto enim eum cum fratribus.
12. As touching our brother Apollos, I greatly desired him to come unto you with the brethren: but his will was not at all to come at this time; but he will come when he shall have convenient time.
12. Porro de Apollo fratre, multum hortatus sum illum, ut veniret ad vos cum fratribus, at omnino non fuit voluntas nunc eundi: veniet autem, quam opportunitatem nactus erit.
entries.710ade38e24e41b8fdaa6dad02742157e309fee5: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.8" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.16.8" sID="gen120526" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8.</hi> <hi type="italic">I will remain.</hi> From this statement I have argued above, that this epistle was sent from Ephesus, rather than from Philippi. For the probability is, that the Apostle speaks of the place in which he was at the time, and not of a place, in going to which he would require to make a long circuit; and farther, in passing through Macedonia, <note n="163"> <div sID="gen120528" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">En passant de Philippes par Macedone</foreign>;” — “In passing from Philippi through Macedonia.”<div eID="gen120528" type="x-p"/> </note> it would have been necessary to leave Corinth when already in the neighborhood of it, and cross the sea in order to reach Ephesus. He accordingly tells them beforehand that he will <hi type="italic">remain at Ephesus until Pentecost, </hi>adding the reason — in order that they may wait for him the more patiently. Erasmus has preferred to render it — <hi type="italic">until the fiftieth day, </hi>influenced by frivolous conjectures rather than by any solid argument. He objects, that there was as yet no day of Pentecost appointed among Christians, as it is now celebrated; and this I grant. He says, that it ought not to be understood as referring to the Jewish solemnity, because in various instances he annuls and condemns the superstitious observance of days. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gal.4.10">Galatians 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.14.5">Romans 14:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Col.2.16 Bible:Col.2.17">Colossians 2:16, 17</reference>.) I do not concede to him, however, that Paul celebrated that day at Ephesus from being influenced by a superstitious regard to the day, but because there would be a larger assembly at that time, and he hoped that, in that way, an opportunity would be presented to him of propagating the gospel. Thus, when he was hastening forward to Jerusalem, he assigned as the reason of his haste, <hi type="italic">that he might arrive there at Pentecost, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.16">Acts 20:16</reference>;) but while others presented themselves there for the purpose of sacrificing according to the ritual of the law, he himself had another object in view — that his ministry might be the more useful in proportion to the largeness of the attendance. It were, however, an excessively poor meaning to understand Paul here as simply specifying fifty days. Besides, when he expressly says <foreign xml:lang="el">τὴν πεντηκοστήν</foreign> <hi type="italic">(the Pentecost,) </hi>he cannot but be understood as speaking of a particular day. As to this festival, see <reference osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.16">Leviticus 23:16</reference><div eID="gen120527" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.8" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120526" osisID="1Cor.16.8" type="section"/>
entries.2ffd1440d9388c62782edf85fa1506eb6a4c5f5d: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.9" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.16.9" sID="gen120529" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120530" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9.</hi> <hi type="italic">For a great and effectual door is opened to me. </hi>He assigns two reasons for remaining for a longer time at Ephesus — 1st, Because an opportunity is afforded him there of furthering the gospel; and 2dly, Because, in consequence of the great number of <hi type="italic">adversaries </hi>that were there, his presence was particularly required. “I shall do much good by prolonging my stay here for a little while, and were I absent, Satan would do much injury.” In the first clause, he makes use of a metaphor that is quite in common use, when he employs the term <hi type="italic">door </hi>as meaning <hi type="italic">an opportunity. </hi>For the Lord opened up a way for him for the furtherance of the gospel. He calls this a <hi type="italic">great </hi>door, because he could gain many. He calls it <hi type="italic">effectual, </hi>inasmuch as the Lord blessed his labor, and rendered his doctrine <hi type="italic">effectual </hi>by the power of His Spirit. We see, then, how this holy man <note n="164"> <div sID="gen120531" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ce sainct Apostre</foreign>;” — “This holy Apostle.”<div eID="gen120531" type="x-p"/> </note> sought everywhere Christ’s glory, and did not select a place with a view to his own convenience or his own pleasure; but simply looked to this — <hi type="italic">where </hi>he might do most good, and serve his Lord with most abundant fruit; and in addition to this, he did not merely not shrink back from hardships, but presented himself, of his own accord, where he saw that he would have to contend more keenly, and with greater difficulty. For the reason why he <hi type="italic">remained</hi> <note n="165"> <div sID="gen120532" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">En Ephese</foreign>;” — “In Ephesus.”<div eID="gen120532" type="x-p"/> </note> was, that <hi type="italic">many adversaries</hi> were at hand; and the better equipped he was for enduring their assault, he required to be so much the better prepared, and the more resolute.<div eID="gen120530" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.9" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120529" osisID="1Cor.16.9" type="section"/>
entries.a182271a4e50791f096e148d2d77833183ef06d8: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.10" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.16.10" sID="gen120533" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120534" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10.</hi> <hi type="italic">But if Timothy come.</hi> He speaks as if he were not as yet certain as to his coming. Now he charges them as to Timothy, so that he may be with them in safety — not as though he were in danger of his life among them, but because he would have enemies of Christ <note n="166"> <div sID="gen120535" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Beaucoup d’ennemis de Christ</foreign>;” — “Many enemies of Christ.”<div eID="gen120535" type="x-p"/> </note> to oppose him. He wishes, therefore, that they should carefully take heed that no injury be done to him.<div eID="gen120534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120536" type="x-p"/>He adds the reason — for he <hi type="italic">worketh the work of the Lord</hi> Hence we infer, that the Church of Christ ought to be concerned for the preservation of the lives of ministers. And assuredly, it is reasonable, that, in proportion as an individual is endowed with superior gifts for the edification of believers, and applies himself to it the more strenuously, his life ought to be so much dearer to us.<div eID="gen120536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120537" type="x-p"/>The clause — <hi type="italic">as I also do, </hi>is made use of, either to express his <hi type="italic">excellence, </hi>or simply to point out the similarity as to office, inasmuch as both labored in the word.<div eID="gen120537" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120533" osisID="1Cor.16.10" type="section"/>
entries.d84248c92e010c2e0c37a89d19bf1b43da324251: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.16.11" sID="gen120538" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120539" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11.</hi> <hi type="italic">Let no man, therefore, despise him</hi> Here we have a <hi type="italic">second </hi>charge, <hi type="italic">that they may not despise </hi>him — perhaps because he was as yet of a youthful age, which usually draws forth less respect. He wishes them, therefore, to take care, that there be no hinderance in the way of this faithful minister of Christ being held in due esteem — unless, perhaps, it be that Paul reckoned this very thing to be an evidence of contempt, if they were not concerned, as it became them to be, in reference to his life. This injunction, however, appears to include something farther, that they should not undervalue Timothy, from ignorance of his worth.<div eID="gen120539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120540" type="x-p"/>In the <hi type="italic">third </hi>place, he charges them to <hi type="italic">conduct him forward in peace, </hi>or, in other words, <hi type="italic">safe from all harm, </hi>for <hi type="italic">peace </hi>here means safety.<div eID="gen120540" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.11" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120538" osisID="1Cor.16.11" type="section"/>
entries.ced707fc8740763b98e7e091c891869a67e2fee5:
12. As to our brother Apollos. He had succeeded Paul in the work of building up the Corinthians; and hence he has in previous passages ascribed to him the office of watering. (1 Corinthians 3:6, and Acts 19:1.) He now states a reason why he does not come with the others, and he states the reason of this, in order that the Corinthians may not suspect that he had been hindered by him. For the better he was known by them, they were so much the more favourably disposed towards him, and they would be the more ready to conjecture, that matters had been designedly contrived, that he should not go to them, in consequence of offense having been taken.
“Que sainct Paul se sentant offense par les Corinthiens, auoit attitre cela tout expres, qu’ Apollos n’allast point vers eux;” — “That St. Paul feeling offended with the Corinthians, had intentionally brought it about, that Apollos should not go to them.”
They might, at least, be prepared to inquire among themselves: “Why has he sent these persons to us rather than Apollos?” He answers, that it was not owing to him, inasmuch as he entreated him; but he promises that he will come as soon as he has opportunity.
1 Corinthians 16:13-24
13. Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
13. Vigilate, state in fide, viriliter agite, robusti estote.
14. Let all your things be done with charity.
14. Omnia vestra in caritate fiant.
15. I beseech you, brethren, (ye know the house of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints,)
15. Hortor autem vos, fratres, nostis domum Stephanae, primitias esse Achaiae, atque ut se in ministerium sanctorum ordinaverint:
16. That ye submit yourselves unto such, and to every one that helpeth with us, and laboureth.
16. Ut etiam subiecti sitis tallbus, et omnibus qui cooperantur et laborant.
17. I am glad of the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus: for that which was lacking on our part they have supplied.
17. Gaudeo autem de praesentia Stephanie, et Fortunati, et Achaici: quia quod deerat a vobis, ipsi suppleverunt.
18. For they have refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them that are such.
18. Refocillarunt enim spiritum meum et vestrum: agnoscite ergo tales.
19. The churches of Asia salute you. Aquila and Priscilla salute you much in the Lord, with the church that is in their house.
19. Salutant vos Ecclesiae Asiae: salutant vos multum in Domino Aquila et Priscilla cum domestica eorum Ecclesia.
20. All the brethren greet you. Greet ye one another with an holy kiss.
20. Salutant vos fratres omnes: salutate vos invicem in osculo sancto.
21. The salutation of me Paul with mine own hand.
21. Salutatio mea manu Pauli.
22. If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha.
22. Si quis non amat Dominum Iesum Christum, sit anathema maranatha.
23. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
23. Gratia Domini Iesu Christi sit vobiscum.
24. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen.
24. Dilectio mea cum vobis omnibus in Christo Iesu. Amen.
The first epistle to the Corinthians was written from Philippi by Stephanas, and Fortunatus, and Achaicus, and Timotheus.
Ad Corinthios prior missa fuit e Philippis per Stephanam, et Fortunatum, et Andronicum, et Timotheum.
It appears from Hug (in his treatise on the antiquity of the Vatican version) that the subscription to this epistle in that version is as follows — προς Κορινθιους ά ενραφη απο Εφεσου — The first to the Corinthians was written from Ephesus. This, it will be observed, favors the view taken by Calvin of the statement made by Paul in 1 Corinthians 16:8. — Ed.
entries.6434a08d48c15b07ba95a1a15562e3a13794d935: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.16.13" sID="gen120574" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120575" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13.</hi> <hi type="italic">Watch ye</hi>. A short exhortation, but of great weight. He exhorts them to <hi type="italic">watch, </hi>in order that Satan may not oppress them, finding them off their guard. For as the warfare is incessant, the <hi type="italic">watching </hi>requires to be incessant too. Now watchfulness of spirit is this — when, free and disentangled from earthly cares, we meditate on the things of God. For as the body is weighed down by <hi type="italic">surfeiting and drunkenness, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.21.34">Luke 21:34</reference>,) so as to be fit for nothing, so the cares and lusts of the world, idleness or carelessness, are like a spiritual surfeiting that overpowers the mind. <note n="169"> <div sID="gen120576" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Sont comme vne yurongnerie spirituelle, qui assopit et estourdit l’entendement</foreign>;” — “Are like a spiritual drunkenness, which makes the mind drowsy and stupid.”<div eID="gen120576" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen120575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120577" type="x-p"/>The <hi type="italic">second </hi>thing is that they <hi type="italic">persevere in the faith, </hi>or that they hold fast the faith, so as to <hi type="italic">stand firm; </hi>because that is the foundation on which we rest. It is certain, however, that he points out the means of perseverance — by resting upon God with a firm faith.<div eID="gen120577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120578" type="x-p"/>In the <hi type="italic">third </hi>exhortation, which is much of the same nature, he stirs them up to manly fortitude. And, as we are naturally weak, he exhorts them <hi type="italic">fourthly to </hi>strengthen themselves, or gather strength. For where we render it <hi type="italic">be strong, </hi>Paul makes use of only one word, which is equivalent to <hi type="italic">strengthen yourselves.</hi><div eID="gen120578" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120574" osisID="1Cor.16.13" type="section"/>
entries.6756ebca1375f1400d90a4577ddfb5149303ea3d: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.14" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.16.14" sID="gen120579" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120580" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">14.</hi> <hi type="italic">Let all your things be done in love</hi> Again he repeats what is the rule in all those transactions, in which we have dealings with one another. He wishes, then, that <hi type="italic">love </hi>shall be the directress; because the Corinthians erred chiefly in this respect — that every one looked to himself without caring for others.<div eID="gen120580" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.14" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120579" osisID="1Cor.16.14" type="section"/>
entries.138a142062ab981f95ebf7b2279c7a7f8e1b5f4c: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.15" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.16.15" sID="gen120581" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120582" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15.</hi> <hi type="italic">Ye know the house of Stephanas</hi> We know, from daily experience, of what advantage it is, that those should have the highest authority, whom God has adorned with the most distinguished gifts. Accordingly, if we wish to secure the welfare of the Church, let us always take care that honor be conferred upon the good: let their counsels have the greatest weight; let others give way to them, and allow themselves to be governed by their prudence. This Paul does in this instance, when admonishing the Corinthians to show respect to the <hi type="italic">house of Stephanas. </hi>Some manuscripts add, <hi type="italic">and Fortunatus.</hi> <note n="170"> <div sID="gen120583" type="x-p"/> The Alex. and Copt. MSS. <hi type="italic">read</hi> — <hi type="italic">and Fortunatus. </hi>The Vulgate <hi type="italic">reads</hi> — <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">Fortunatum et Achaicum</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">; </hi>in accordance with which the rendering in Wiclif (1380) is, <hi type="italic">Ye knowen the hous of stephart and of fortunati, and acacie. </hi>The Rheims version (1582) reads — You <hi type="italic">know the house of Ste-phanas and of Fortunatus.</hi> — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen120583" type="x-p"/> </note> For God manifests himself to us when he shows us the gifts of his Spirit. Hence, if we would not appear to be despisers of God, let us voluntarily <hi type="italic">submit ourselves </hi>to those, on whom God has conferred superior gifts.<div eID="gen120582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen120584" type="x-p"/>Now, that they may be the more inclined to put honor upon <hi type="italic">that house, </hi>(for as to the other, it appears to me to be, in this place at least, a spurious addition,) he reminds them that they were the <hi type="italic">first-fruits of Achaia, </hi>that is, that the household of Stephanas were the first that had embraced the gospel. Not indeed as though the first in order of time were in every case superior to the others, but where there is perseverance along with this, it is with good reason, that honor is conferred upon those, who have in a manner paved the way for the gospel by promptitude of faith. It must be observed, however, that he dignifies with this honorable title those, who had consecrated to believers their services and resources. For the same reason, he bestows commendation a little afterwards upon Fortunatus and Achaicus, that, in proportion to a man’s superiority of excellence, <note n="171"> <div sID="gen120585" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Selon que chacun estoit plus homme de bien et vertueux</foreign>;” — “In proportion as an individual was an honorable and virtuous man.”<div eID="gen120585" type="x-p"/> </note> he might be held so much the more in esteem, that he might be able to do the more good. Farther, in order that the Corinthians may be the more disposed to love them, he says, that <hi type="italic">what had been wanting</hi> on the part of their entire Church <hi type="italic">had been compensated for </hi>by their vicarious services.<div eID="gen120584" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.15" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120581" osisID="1Cor.16.15" type="section"/>
entries.4240cefedeb07e57fd70589815fd1ec5cc605061: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.19" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.16.19" sID="gen120586" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120587" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">19.</hi> <hi type="italic">With the Church that is in their house</hi> A magnificent eulogium, inasmuch as the name of the Church is applied to a single family! At the same time it is befitting, that all the families of the pious should be regulated in such a manner as to be so many little Churches. As to the term <hi type="italic">Congregation, </hi>which Erasmus has used in preference, it is foreign to Paul’s design; for it was not his intention to designate a crowd of persons by a mere common term, but to speak in honorable terms of the management of a Christian household. His saluting them in the name of Aquila and Priscilla, confirms what I have noticed above — that the Epistle was written at Ephesus, not at Philippi. For Luke informs us, that they remained at Ephesus, when Paul went elsewhere. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.19">Acts 18:19</reference>.)<div eID="gen120587" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.19" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120586" osisID="1Cor.16.19" type="section"/>
entries.799bfb9c8d3ac65e6e392943feecefdddca332ae: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.20" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.16.20" sID="gen120588" type="section"/> <div sID="gen120589" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20.</hi> <hi type="italic">Salute one another with a holy kiss.</hi> The practice of kissing was very common among the Jews, as is manifest from the Scriptures. In <hi type="italic">Greece, </hi>though it was not so common and customary, it was by no means unknown; but the probability is, that Paul speaks here of a solemn kiss, with which they saluted each other in the sacred assembly. For I could easily believe, that from the times of the Apostles a kiss was used in connection with the administration of the Supper; <note n="172"> <div sID="gen120590" type="x-p"/> “That the Apostle,” says Dr. Brown in his Commentary on 1st Peter, “meant the members of the Churches, on receiving this Epistle, to salute one another is certain; that he meant, that at all their religious meetings they should do so, is not <hi type="italic">improbable. </hi>That he meant to make this an everlasting ordinance in all Christian Churches, though it has sometimes been asserted, has never been proved, and is by no means likely. That the practice prevailed extensively, perhaps universally, in the earlier ages, is established on satisfactory evidence. ‘After the prayers,’ says Justin Martyr, who lived in the earlier part of the second century, giving an account in his Apology of the religious customs of the Christians — ’after the prayers, we embrace each other with a kiss.’ Tertullian speaks of it as an ordinary part of the religious services of the Lord’s day; and in the Apostolical Constitutions, as they are <hi type="italic">termed, </hi>the manner in which it was performed is particularly described. ‘Then let the men apart, and the women apart, salute each other with a kiss in the Lord.’ Origen’s Note on <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.16.16">Romans 16:16</reference>, is: ‘From this passage the custom was delivered to the Churches, that, after prayer, the brethren should salute one another with a kiss.’ This token of love was generally given at the Holy Supper. It was likely, from the prevalence of this custom, that the calumny of Christians indulging in licentiousness at their religious meetings originated; and it is not improbable that, in order to remove everything like an occasion to calumniators, the practice which, though in itself innocent, had become not for the use of edifying, was <hi type="italic">discontinued.”</hi> — <hi type="italic">Brown’s </hi>Expository Discourses on 1st Peter, volume in. pages 309, 310. “It is remarkable that, by the testimony of Suetonius, an edict was published by one of the Roman Emperors, for the abolition of this practice among his subjects, — perhaps in order to check abuses, for the prevention of which our Apostle enjoins that it shall be a <hi type="italic">holy salutation.”</hi> — <hi type="italic">Chalmers </hi>on the Romans, volume in. page 428. — Ed.<div eID="gen120590" type="x-p"/> </note> in place of which, among nations that were somewhat averse to the practice of kissing, there crept in the custom of kissing the patine. <note n="173"> <div sID="gen120591" type="x-p"/> By the <foreign xml:lang="fr"><hi type="italic">patine</hi></foreign> or <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">paten</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">, </hi>is meant the <hi type="italic">plate </hi>or <hi type="italic">salver </hi>on which the wafer or bread was placed in the observance of the mass. The term is made use of by <hi type="italic">Dr. Stillingfleet </hi>in his “Preservative from Popery,” (title 7, chapter 5,) in speaking of the practice of the Church of Rome in the adoration of the host: “The priest in every mass, as soon as he has consecrated the bread and wine, with bended knees, he adores the sacrament; that which he has consecrated, that very thing which is before him, upon the <foreign xml:lang="fr"><hi type="italic">patine</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">, </hi>and in the chalice; and gives the same worship and subjection, both of body and mind, to it as he could to God or Christ himself.” In <hi type="italic">Young’s </hi>Lectures on Popery, (Loud. 1836,) page 140, the following account is given of the sacrifice of the mass: “Upon the altar is the chalice, or cup, which is to contain the wine, mixed with a little water; and covering the cup is the <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">paten</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">, </hi>or <hi type="italic">plate, </hi>intended to hold the cake or wafer. After an almost endless variety of movements, and forms, and prayers, and readings, the priest goes to the altar, and, taking the cup containing wine and water, with the wafer upon the <hi type="italic">cover,</hi> — <hi type="italic">these </hi>having been before consecrated and transubstantiated into the body and blood of Christ, — he raises his eyes and says, ‘Take, O Holy Trinity, this oblation, which I, unworthy sinner, offer in honor of thee, of the blessed Virgin Mary, and of all the saints, for the salvation of the living, and for the rest and quiet of all the faithful that are dead.’ Then, setting down the chalice, he says, ‘Let this sacrifice be acceptable to Almighty <hi type="italic">God.’” </hi>The name <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">paten</hi></foreign> is preserved in the English Liturgy to this day. In the prayer of consecration, in the communion service — in connection with the words, <hi type="italic">“who, </hi>in the same night that he was betrayed, took bread,” it is said, <hi type="italic">“here </hi>the priest is to take the <hi type="italic">paten </hi>into his hands.” Calvin, when commenting upon <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.16.16">Romans 16:16</reference>, after having stated that it was customary among the primitive Christians, before partaking of the Lord’s Supper, to kiss each other in token of sacred friendship, and afterwards to give alms, says, <hi type="italic">“</hi><foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">Hinc </hi>fluxit ritus ille, qui hodie est apud Papistas, <hi type="italic">osculandoe patents, </hi>et conferendse oblationis. Quorum alterum merae est superstitionis, sine ullo fructu: alterum non alto facit, nisi ad explendam sacerdotum avari-tiam, si tamen expleri posset</foreign>;<hi type="italic">”</hi> — <hi type="italic">“</hi>From this has sprung that ceremony which is at this day among Papists, of <hi type="italic">kissing the patine, </hi>and making an offering. The former is mere superstition without any advantage: the latter serves no purpose, except to <hi type="italic">satisfy </hi>the greed of the priests, if <hi type="italic">satis</hi>fied it can be.” <hi type="italic">­Poole, </hi>in his Annotations on <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.16.16">Romans 16:16</reference>, says, “The primitive Christians did use it” (the <hi type="italic">holy kiss) “in </hi>their assemblies; so <hi type="italic">Tertullian </hi>testifieth, (Lib. Dec.,) and they did it especially in receiving the Eucharist. So Chrysostom witnesseth, (Hom. 77 in <reference osisRef="Bible:John.16">John 16</reference>,) ‘we do well,’ saith he, ‘to <hi type="italic">kiss in the mysteries, </hi>that we may become <hi type="italic">one.’</hi> This custom for good reasons is laid down, and the <hi type="italic">Romanists </hi>in room of it, keep up a foolish and superstitious ceremony, which is to <hi type="italic">kiss the pax </hi>in the mass.” — Ed.<div eID="gen120591" type="x-p"/> </note> However this may be, as it was a token of mutual love. I have no doubt, that Paul meant to exhort them to the cultivation of good-will among themselves — not merely in their minds <note n="174"> <div sID="gen120592" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Par affection interieure</foreign>;” — “By inward affection.”<div eID="gen120592" type="x-p"/> </note> and in needful services, but also by that token, provided only it was <hi type="italic">holy, </hi>that is, neither unchaste nor deceitful, <note n="175"> <div sID="gen120593" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ou consistast en mine seulement</foreign>;” — “Or consisted in mere appearance.”<div eID="gen120593" type="x-p"/> </note> — though, at the same time, <hi type="italic">holy </hi>may be taken to mean <hi type="italic">sacred.</hi><div eID="gen120589" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.16.20" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen120588" osisID="1Cor.16.20" type="section"/>

22. If any man love not the Lord Jesus The close of the Epistle consists of three parts. He entreats the grace of Christ in behalf of the Corinthians: he makes a declaration of his love towards them, and, with the severest threatening, he inveighs against those that falsely took upon themselves the Lord’s name, while not loving him from the heart. For he is not speaking of strangers, who avowedly hated the Christian name, but of pretenders and hypocrites, who troubled the Churches for the sake of their own belly, or from empty boasting.
“Ne cherehans que le proufit de lents ventres, et leur propre gloire;” “Seeking only the profit of their bellies, and their own glory.”
On such persons he denounces an anathema, and he also pronounces a curse upon them. It is not certain, however, whether he desires their destruction in the presence of God, or whether he wishes to render them odious — nay, even execrable, in the view of believers. Thus in Galatians 1:8, when pronouncing one who corrupts the Gospel to be accursed,
Calvin, when commenting on Galatians 1:8, remarks that the original term there employed, anathema, denotes cursing, and answers to the Hebrew word חרם; and he explains the expression — “let him be accursed,” as meaning, “Let him be held by you as accursed.”
he does not mean that he was rejected or condemned by God, but he declares that he is to be abhorred by us. I expound it in a simple way as follows: “Let them perish and be cut off, as being the pests of the Church.” And truly, there is nothing that is more pernicious, than that class of persons, who prostitute a profession of piety to their own depraved affections. Now he points out the origin of this evil, when he says, that they do not love Christ, for a sincere and earnest love to Christ will not suffer us to give occasion of offense to brethren.
“Car si nous aimons Christ purement, et a bon escient, ce nous sera vne bride qui nons retiendra de donner scandale a nos fieres;” — “For if we love Christ sincerely and in good earnest, this will be a bridle to restrain us from giving offense to our brethren.”
What he immediately adds — Maranatha, is somewhat more difficult. Almost all of the ancients are agreed, that they are Syriac terms.
“Que ce sont mots empruntez de la langue Syrienne;” — “That they are words borrowed from the Syriac language.”
Jerome, however, explains it: The Lord cometh; while others render it, At the coming of the Lord, or, Until the Lord comes. Every one, however, I think, must see how silly and puerile is the idea, that the Apostle spoke to Greeks in the Syriac tongue, when meaning to say — The Lord has come. Those who translate it, at the coming of the Lord, do so on mere conjecture; and besides, there is not much plausibility in that interpretation. How much more likely it is, that this was a customary form of expression among the Hebrews, when they wished to excommunicate any one. For the Apostles never speak in foreign tongues, except when they repeat anything in the person of another, as for example, Eli, Eli, lammah sabathani, (Matthew 27:46,) Talitha cumi, (Mark 5:41,) and Ephphata, (Mark 7:34,) or when they make use of a word that has come into common use, as Amen — Hosanna. “Henrici Bullingeri, Ecclesiastae Tigurini, spectatisa, doctrine, pictaris, et eximii candoris viri, memoriae;” — (To the memory of HENRY Bullinger, ecclesiastick of Tigurum, a man most distinguished for learning and piety, and extraordinary candour.)

               <ns0:head>CHAP. XVI.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 NOw concerning <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 24.17. 2 Cor. 9.1, 2, 12.</ns0:note> the collection for the Saints <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The business of relieving the poor Members of the Church, is a moral Duty, <ns0:hi>a Sacrifice with which God is well pleased</ns0:hi>; our Faith must work by this Love. The Apostle, in several Epi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stles, was very sollicitous about this: he mentioneth it <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 15.26. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 2.10. as well as in this Epistle. Besides, that our Saviour had foretold, That the state of the Church would be such, that they should have the poor always with them. <ns0:hi>Agabus, Acts</ns0:hi> 11.28. had prophesied of a Famine, which (some think) raged at this time; and besides, the Persecution at <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> had scat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tered the Brethren abroad, and being out of their Country and imployments, they could not but be at a loss for a livelihood; and so need the charitable contribution of other Churches under better circumstances, as they were at this time in <ns0:hi>Greece.</ns0:hi> The Churches of <ns0:hi>Galatia</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Macedonia</ns0:hi> had been very liberal this way; and the Apostle, by their Example, quickens the Chur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ches both at <ns0:hi>Rome</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Corinth, Rom</ns0:hi> 15.26. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.4.</ns0:note>, as I have given order to the churches of Galatia, even so do ye <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">As to this he had (as he saith) <ns0:hi>given order to the Churches of Gala<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tia,</ns0:hi> which, it is thought, he did in his journey through <ns0:hi>Gala<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tia, Acts</ns0:hi> 16.6. and he ordereth the Church at <ns0:hi>Corinth</ns0:hi> to fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />low that Order, which followeth.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 20.7. Rev. 1.10.</ns0:note> Upon the first <ns0:hi>day</ns0:hi> of the week <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">From hence both divers of the Ancients, and very many late Divines, argue for the change of the Sabbath from the se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venth day of the week to the first. It is plain from hence, that the Gospel-Churches were wont to assemble upon that day, (nor do we read in Scripture of any Assembly of Christians for religious Worship on any other day.) On this day the Apostle orders Collections for the poor Saints to be made, accordingly as God had prospered any in their imployments; he directeth that they should every one lay by him something, not doing what he did with any oftentation, but having it ready when it should be called for: this he calls a <ns0:hi>Treasuring,</ns0:hi> (so it is in the Greek) treasuring; monies laid by for charitable uses are Trea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sures, both with respect to those for whom they are laid up, and also for our selves; for he that giveth to the poor, layeth up for himself Treasures in Heaven.</ns0:note>, let every one of you lay by him in store, as <ns0:hi>God</ns0:hi> hath pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spered him, that there be no gatherings when I come <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">He would have <ns0:hi>no gatherings when he came,</ns0:hi> either to avoid the scandal of his being charge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />able to them, or that he would have no delay; but when he came, it might be in a readiness to be presently sent away.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Cor. 8.16, 19.</ns0:note> when I come, whomsoever you shall approve by <ns0:hi>your</ns0:hi> letters, them will I send to bring your <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>gist.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> liberality to Jerusalem <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The word here translated <ns0:hi>Liberality,</ns0:hi> is the same which sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifieth <ns0:hi>Grace</ns0:hi>; their Charity is called by that Name, either be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause it flowed from their <ns0:hi>free Love</ns0:hi> towards their poor Brethren, (though living at a great distance from them;) or because their sense of the free Love and Grace of God to them, was that which moved them to that charitable act, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.9.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 And if it be meet that I go also, they shall go with me <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">To incourage them to the freer and more liberal Contri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bution, he promiseth them himself to go along with those that carried it, (if it were thought meet.)</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 Now I will come unto you, when <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 19.21<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> I shall pass through Macedonia: For I do pass through Macedonia <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Whether <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> according to this promise, did go to <ns0:hi>Co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rinth,</ns0:hi> some question; because of what we read, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.15, 16. But others think, that he speaketh there of another jour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ney which he intended thither; and that he did go in a fulfil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ling of this promise, because we read, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 19. that he went into <ns0:hi>Achaia,</ns0:hi> and spent there a considerable time; during which, it is very probable that he did not omit to visit the Church of <ns0:hi>Co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rinth.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 And it may be that I will abide, yea, and win<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter with you, that you may bring me on my jour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ney whithersoever I go <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">He did stay in <ns0:hi>Macedonia</ns0:hi> three months, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 20.3. but it is believed some things hindered him, that he did not winter at <ns0:hi>Corinth.</ns0:hi> It was the custom for some Members of the Gospel-Churches, to accompany the Apostles some part of their way when they went from them to any other places, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 15.3. & 17.15. & 20.38. in token of their kindness and respect to them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 For I will not see you now by the way, but I trust to tarry a while with you, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 18.21. Chap. 4.19. Jam. 4.15.</ns0:note> if the Lord per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mit <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">I will not see you in my passage into <ns0:hi>Macedonia,</ns0:hi> for then I shall have no time to stay long with you; and I hope to gain a time when I shall stay longer with you; but all this must be understood with submission to Gods Will, who can hinder, and order my journies, and determine my purposes as he pleaseth. <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> teaches us, when we declare our resolutions to go to this or that place, to add, <ns0:hi>If God will</ns0:hi>; and our Apostle observeth that Rule, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.10.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 But I will tarry at Ephesus until Pentecost <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">He altered this resolution afterward; for, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 20.16. be <ns0:hi>hasted, if it were possible, to get to Ierusalem by Pentecost.</ns0:hi> Pen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tecost was a Jewish Feast, and not named here as a Feast then celebrated by Christians, but as a known period of time; for the Jews computing time from their Festivals, Christians who lived amongst them, and had some of them been converted from their Religion, computed also their time from the Jewish <ns0:hi>Festivals.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 14.27. 2 Cor. 2.12.</ns0:note> For a great door and effectual is opened to me <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">For God hath opened to me at <ns0:hi>Ephesus</ns0:hi> a great opportunity to preach the Gospel, which I have reason to hope will also be effectual for the Conversion of many Souls. What this door of hope was, whether God had let him know there were many Souls in that place prepared for receiving the Gospel; or that some eminent Persons for Authority or Learning, whom many were like to follow, were there already converted; or that he looked upon that famous City as like to be a place where many might be converted, is not told us.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:hi>there are</ns0:hi> many adversaries <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>And</ns0:hi> (saith the Apostle) <ns0:hi>there are many Adversaries,</ns0:hi> (as it will appear to those that read <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 19, & 20.) therefore there was need of the presence of the Apostle himself, whose Authority might better stop their mouths, than the more inferior Pastors could. What would have affrighted others from going or staying there, this great Apostle mentions as an Argument to cause him to make haste to go thither, and to tarry there for some time.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Now if Timotheus come, see that he may be with you without fear <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">He had told them, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 4.17. That he had sent <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> unto them, whom he there calleth his <ns0:hi>beloved Son, and faithful in the Lord.</ns0:hi> Here he bespeaketh his welcome and security. It is probable he had it in Commission from <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> to visit divers others Churches in his journey to them; and therefore he speak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth of his coming as uncertain, but chargeth them, that if he did come, they would take care of him, that he might not be exposed to danger or trouble from any Party amongst them.</ns0:note>: for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>6.21. Phil. 2.20, 2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 1 Thess. 3.2.</ns0:note> he worketh the work of the Lord, as I also <ns0:hi>do</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">For (saith he) he is a Minister of the Gospel, and ingaged in the same work of the Lord that I am.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 Let no man therefore despise him <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Either, because he is a very young man, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.12, 13. or upon any other account.</ns0:note>: but con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />duct him forth in peace, that he may come unto me <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">But when he cometh away, shew him the respect you use to shew me, conduct him in his way.</ns0:note>; for I look for him with the brethren <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">For I have need of his help here, in carrying on the business of the Gospel; and therefore I with the Brethren here expect him; or I expect him with the rest of the Brethren, who are in like manner imployed abroad in carrying about the Gospel.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:458" />12 As touching <ns0:hi>our</ns0:hi> brother Apollos, I greatly desired him to come unto you with the brethren, but his will was not at all to come at this time: but he will come when he shall have a convenient time <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Apollos</ns0:hi> (as may be seen <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 18.27.) was known to them, and had been a Preacher amongst them, and was grateful to many of them; he was an <ns0:hi>eloquent man, mighty in the Scrip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tures, instructed in the way of the Lord, and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ervent in the Spirit, Acts</ns0:hi> 18.24, 25, 26, 27, 28. he was one of those from whom some of this Church denominated themselves, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 3.4. For these reasons <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> would have perswaded him to go and visit this Church (which some think that he had left, because of those contentions and divisions, which were amongst them) but he had no mind to go at that time; though it is said, that he af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terwards did return again to them, when <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> by his Epistle, had quieted those divisions, and allayed their heats.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 Watch ye <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Watching, in its usual acception, signifieth a forbearing of sleep; and that in order to some End. Sin is set out under the notion of <ns0:hi>Sleep, Eph.</ns0:hi> 5.14. so that spiritual watching signifies a diligent abstaining from sin, and from whatsoever may be to us a temptation to sin against God, in order to the perfecting of Holiness, and the obtaining life and immortality.</ns0:note>, stand fast in the faith <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Be stea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dy in the profession of the Truth, and holding close to the Doctrine of Faith.</ns0:note>, quit you like men: be strong <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">You are as Souldiers fighting against the World, the Flesh, and the Devil; do not behave your selves like children, whom the least opposition will terrifie and throw down; but like men, with a spiritual courage and forti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tude, becoming such who have so good a Captain, and so good a Cause</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 Let all your things be done with charity <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Charity (as hath been before discoursed) is a term com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prehensive both of <ns0:hi>Love to God,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>to our Neighbour</ns0:hi>; the fai<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lure of this in their divisions and contentions, and satisfying their own judgments and humors, without regard to the Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sciences of others, and having no regard to the profit of others, is that which the Apostle, in this Epistle, had once and again blamed in the Members of this Church; in the conclusion of his Epistle, he therefore again recommends to them the getting and exercising of this habit.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 I beseech you, brethren, ye know the hou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shold of Stephanas, that it is <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 16.5.</ns0:note> the first-fruits of Achaia <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Of this <ns0:hi>Stephanas</ns0:hi> we read before <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 1.16. his Family was one of those few Families which <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> baptized: he is here called the <ns0:hi>First-fruits of Achaia,</ns0:hi> because (as it should seem) he was one of the first of all those who in that Country received the Gospel.</ns0:note>, and that they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the Saints <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">He further saith of him, That he had given up him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self to the Ministry of the Saints, either in preaching the Gospel, or (which is more probable) in the proper imployment of a <ns0:hi>Deacon,</ns0:hi> in relieving such amongst the Saints (whether of that, or other Churches) that were in want.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 13.19.</ns0:note> That ye submit your selves unto such, and to every one that helpeth with <ns0:hi>us,</ns0:hi> and laboureth <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">He adviseth them to reverence him, and all such as were helpers and labourers of that nature, and wrought with the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stles in the work of the Gospel.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 I am glad of the coming of Stephanas, For<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tunatus, and Achaicus: for that which was lacking on your part, they have supplied.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 For they have refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore <ns0:note place="margin">Thess. 5.12.</ns0:note> acknowledge ye them that are such <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">It should seem that this Church had sent these three Persons to <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> at this time (as most think) at <ns0:hi>Ephesus,</ns0:hi> to acquaint him with the state of their Churches; these men supplied the want of that whole Churches coming, or they made a report to the Apostle of the <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> more fully, than they had done in their Letters. He adds, That they had <ns0:hi>refreshed his Spirit,</ns0:hi> not with bringing him any money, (for the Apostle hath told us, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 9.15. that he gloried in this, That he had preached the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spel to them freely, without being any charge to them) but by their visit, and the Conference that he had had with them about the state of that Church. The Apostle addeth, That they had refreshed their <ns0:hi>Spirits</ns0:hi> also; intimating, that their joy was his, and that what was a refreshing to him, ought also to be so to them: he therefore recommendeth these men, and such as they were, to be reverenced and respected by this Church.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 The churches of Asia salute you <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">He meaneth the lesser <ns0:hi>Asi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:hi>; in which was <ns0:hi>Ephesus</ns0:hi>; from whence it is more probable, (according to the <ns0:hi>Arabick</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Syriack</ns0:hi> Opinion) that this Epistle was written, than from <ns0:hi>Philippi,</ns0:hi> (ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to the Copy followed by our Translators) And that which further adds to that probability, is, That</ns0:note>: Aquila and Priscilla salute you much in the Lord <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle mentioneth the Salutations of <ns0:hi>Aquila</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Priscilla,</ns0:hi> as per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons that were at that time with him; now that they lived at <ns0:hi>Ephesus,</ns0:hi> or at least went thither with <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> and tarried there, appeareth from <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 18.19. their saluting the Church of <ns0:hi>Corinth</ns0:hi> in the Lord, signifies their wishing them all spiritual blessings in, and from Christ.</ns0:note>, with the church that is in their house <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">But what is meant by the <ns0:hi>Church in their house,</ns0:hi> which joyned with <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> in this Salutation, is not so plain: we read the like, <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 4.15. of the Church in <ns0:hi>Nymphas</ns0:hi> his house; and in <ns0:hi>Philemon</ns0:hi>'s house, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 2. and the same again of this <ns0:hi>Aquila</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Priscilla, Rom.</ns0:hi> 16.5. Some think that it signifieth no more, than that their whole Families had received the Christian Faith. Others think, that divers other Christians sojourned with them; others, that the Church was wont to meet in some room in their house: but the last is not proba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble, either that in those times the Church kept their Meetings in any one stated place, or that Christians then had such spaci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous houses as could afford a room large enough for the whole Church to meet in.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 All the Brethren greet you: Greet you one another with an holy kiss <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This proveth no more, than that as it is in use with us, to salute one another with a kiss when we meet; so it was in use in those Times and Countries to do the like, in token of Love and Friendship. It is called the Kiss of Love, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 5.14. The Apostle requireth, that in these Salutations they should have chast and holy thoughts. This seemeth to be all meant by the <ns0:hi>Holy Kiss,</ns0:hi> mentioned <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 16.16. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 13.12. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 5.26. and here.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Col. 4.18. 2 Thess. 3.17.</ns0:note> The salutation of <ns0:hi>me</ns0:hi> Paul with my own hand <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">These words are judged to signifie to us, that though the former part of the Epistle was written out of <ns0:hi>Pauls</ns0:hi> Copy by some others; yet the three last verses were wrote by him with his own hand.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Love is an affection of the heart, but discernable by overt acts; the meaning is, If any man, by any notorious acts, de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clareth that he loveth not the Lord Jesus, whether he be an Hypocrite owning the Name of Christ, but living in a contempt of, and disobedience to his Commandments; or an Apostate, who sheweth his want of love to Christ, by denying him in an hour of danger and persecution; or an open Enemy and Perse<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cutor of Christ and his Gospel.</ns0:note>, let him be Anathema, Maran-atha <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Let him be accursed, let him be looked upon as a detestable and abominable person. Some tell us, That the Jews having three Excommunications, this word signifieth their highest degree, by which the person was given up to the Judgment and Vengeance of God: But others say, there is no such term to be found among them, and that the term <ns0:hi>Maran-atha</ns0:hi> signifies no more than, <ns0:hi>The Lord is come.</ns0:hi> Let the Jews and other vain persons say what they will, the Lord is come; and if any love him not, let him be looked on as a detestable person.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 16.20<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> with you <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">That is, the Lord Jesus favour you, and bless you with all spiritual Blessings; this is the Apostles ordinary Salutation, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 16.24.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">As I love you, so I desire to be again beloved of you in Christ sincerely. Or I love you all in Christ, and for Christs sake; or I wish that my Love may abide in, and with you.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p>¶ The first <ns0:hi>epistle</ns0:hi> to the Corinthians was writ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ten from Philippi by Stephanas, and Fortuna<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tus, and Achaicus, and Timotheus.<ns0:note place="bottom">These words are no part of Scripture; and (as was said be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore) it is much more probable, that this Epistle was wrote from <ns0:hi>Ephesus</ns0:hi> than from <ns0:hi>Philippi,</ns0:hi> though it might be sent by these, or some of these men named.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
